A journalistic customer account published by a supplier: what the customer set out to do, how they acted, what happened and how they judge the experience. The customer's voice carries the experience; the writer gives it context and progression.

Apply the shared [web craft brief](../web-craft.md).

## What this genre asks for

Lead with a headline about the customer's benefit or result, then a self-contained ingress. Give enough customer background to understand the situation, what prompted the work, the choices and implementation, the supported results with their qualifications, and the customer's own appraisal. Arrange these for understanding; they need neither a heading each nor a quota of quotations. A next step belongs where the assignment supports it.

Keep the customer an acting party. Name the supplier in third person in the narrative, while quotations retain their speaker's perspective. The publisher's interest is not a licence for unsupported praise or a claim of independent reporting.

Let attributed quotations carry the customer's experience and judgement, with narrative doing the connecting work. A bridge should prepare a quotation rather than pre-say it. Preserve the supplied speech within the quotation policy and the language's conventions.

The appraisal must actually be the customer's; a qualified judgement is sufficient. Where no appraisal or quotable speech is supplied, the gap remains visible and is reported, rather than filled with inferred satisfaction or invented words. A before-and-after result is not by itself evidence of the supplier's effect.

## The technique this genre is ordinarily written with

None.
# Delivery

Every Skill that produces a Text Artifact delivers it the same way. This document is the complete contract: where a result goes, what the response carries when it went somewhere else, when a source file may be replaced instead, what happens when nothing changed, what language a run's own words about the text are written in, and what is refused before anything is written. It is a reference several Skills read rather than a runtime of its own. Each Skill exposes these rules through its own Formal Invocation and owns the names it gives them, so nothing here fixes how an option is spelled; what is fixed is the behaviour behind it.

## The response is the default

The default Output Target is the agent response. A run that keeps the default delivers the complete Text Artifact in the response and changes nothing on the filesystem: it creates no file, touches no file, and makes no directory. That includes scratch files and working copies of the artifact, wherever the Harness says temporary files belong.

A Harness convention identifies where an authorized temporary file belongs; it does not authorize a write. If a run genuinely needs a scratch file while composing, it removes that file before delivery and restores the filesystem to the state in which it found it. Before reporting delivery, the run checks the filesystem locations it used, including the Harness scratch area, and never reports that nothing was written while a copy of the artifact remains on disk.

An Output Target is independent of where the source material came from. Supplying a local file as source material selects no destination, and a run that reads a file still delivers to the response until the caller names somewhere else. Persisting a result is the caller's explicit choice, and making that choice is the whole of the authorization for it.

## An explicit destination

An explicit destination is one filesystem path, and what exists at that path decides what happens to it.

**A path that does not exist** creates exactly that one file and writes the complete Text Artifact into it. Exactly one file: nothing else is created beside it, and no directory is made to hold it.

**A path naming an existing file** overwrites that exact file with the complete Text Artifact. No confirmation and no separate force option is required, and none is offered. Naming the path is the authorization, and demanding a second gesture on top of it would teach that naming a destination means something less than it says.

**A path naming an existing directory** delivers into that directory under a filename the run derives, by the rules below. Choosing a directory selects a place, not a file, so it never overwrites a file already in it.

## Deriving a filename for a directory

A directory destination needs a name, and the name comes from what the run already knows. Take the first of these the run has: the basename of the local file that supplied the Text Artifact, the title of a referenced URL, then the Skill's own working title for the text it created. Reduce it to a name the filesystem accepts, and keep a suitable text extension — the source file's own where it had one, and otherwise the one matching the text's format.

That gives a stem and an extension, and the stem stays as it is for every delivery into that directory. Where nothing exists at the derived name, that name is the file written. Where something exists there, the existing file is never overwritten: keep the original stem and take the first free numbered candidate in ascending order, beginning at `-2`. So `my-file.md`, `my-file-2.md`, `my-file-3.md` are one sequence, growing by one name at a time.

A numbered candidate is never adopted as the new stem. A third delivery into a directory already holding the first two is `my-file-3.md` and never `my-file-2-2.md`, whose stem would fork the sequence in two and leave the directory recording how many times the same text arrived rather than which arrival it was. Ascending order with the first free name also means a number freed by a deleted file is used again before a higher one is taken.

## What the response carries when a destination was named

A run that delivers to an explicit destination does not repeat the Text Artifact in the response. The response says where the text went — the derived filename included, where the destination was a directory — and carries what the file cannot: the findings the run reports beside the text, and which of them are unresolved. Naming a destination is saying where the text goes, and printing it again spends output on what the caller is already holding, doubly so when the file just written holds it too.

That holds whether or not the pass changed anything. A run that writes a file byte-identical to the source it read reports the destination and says the text needed no work, and does not become the one run that echoes a text the caller had before it started. The response is the default target precisely because a run that names no destination has nowhere else to put the artifact; naming one moves the text out of the response rather than duplicating it there.

## In-place Editing

In-place Editing replaces the single local file that supplied the Text Artifact with the result, instead of delivering it anywhere else. It is available only to a Skill whose work is to return a changed version of a text the caller already has.

A Skill that creates a new Text Artifact never edits its own source material in place. The brief, the interview, the notes, and the article it draws on are where the text came from and not where it goes; a Skill that could overwrite them would make supplying a file a risk rather than a convenience, and would lose the material the result is answerable to.

In-place Editing requires exactly one writable local source file, and it is mutually exclusive with a separate output option. A run replaces its source or delivers elsewhere, never both, and an invocation asking for both has named two destinations for one text.

It is refused wherever there is no such file to replace. Text supplied inline in the invocation or taken from the conversation is not a file. A URL is not a local file, and fetching one grants no right to write anything back. An uploaded source and a read-only file cannot be replaced. More than one Text Artifact leaves the single file the contract is written around undefined.

An explicit output path equal to the input path is refused in favour of In-place Editing, and the refusal says which gesture to use. Replacing a source then has one recognizable authorization: a reader of an invocation sees that a source is about to be replaced from the request itself, without comparing two paths to discover it.

## When nothing changed

A run may finish with nothing to change, and what it does then follows its destination.

A response-targeted run that changed nothing returns a short no-change status in place of the text when no unresolved findings remain. When findings remain, deliver the complete Text Artifact in the response and report the unresolved findings separately.

An in-place run that changed nothing leaves the source file untouched and returns the short status with any unresolved findings. Rewriting a file with its own contents would make its timestamp claim that something happened.

That status is written in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, so a Swedish text that needed no work is reported on in Swedish.

An explicitly selected different file or directory still receives the complete Text Artifact when nothing changed. Creating that artifact is what was asked for, and a destination left empty because the text needed no work is a request refused without saying so. A directory destination derives its filename and resolves collisions exactly as it would for a changed text, and the response reports the destination without repeating the artifact beside it, exactly as for a run that changed something.

## The language of a report about the text

A run that reports on the text beside the text itself — the findings it carries forward, and which of them are unresolved — writes that report in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, exactly as the no-change status above is written. So a Swedish artifact reviewed from an English-language invocation comes back with Swedish findings, whether the run corrected anything or was asked to correct nothing at all, and one text never produces a status in its own language beside a finding list in another.

Who reads it is what decides this. A report about a text is read by the reader of that text, who has to finish whatever the run left undone, and a report in whichever language the invocation happened to be written in reaches that reader in a language nothing about the text promised. The invocation's language is how the run was asked for; the artifact's language is what the run is about.

## Refusals

Every contradictory, meaningless, or unusable output request is refused before the first side effect. The cases this contract names are more than one Text Artifact where the Skill processes one, an output option together with In-place Editing, an output path equal to the input path, In-place Editing for inline text or a URL or an uploaded or read-only source, and a destination the run cannot write — a path whose parent directory does not exist among them.

Every such check that can be made by reading is made before anything is written, so a refusal leaves no partial effect behind: no file created, none truncated, none renamed, and no directory made. Where a conflict can only be discovered after a legitimate effect, the run stops there and reports the exact partial outcome rather than continuing.

A refusal follows the Collection's ordinary diagnostic and help conventions. It names what was wrong, prints the synopsis of the most specific recognized command page verbatim, and points at that command's own help form. An output option is refused rather than ignored where it has no work to do, a flag accepted and ignored teaching that flags sometimes do nothing.
# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.
# Source and quotation comparison

Check the completed draft before delivery. Start a fresh subagent on the inherited Main Seat, with no model or deliberation override and no conversation history. Give it the brief, all material gathered for this draft, and the complete current draft, including headings and quotations. Supply the actual source text, not your summary or interpretation; source files may be read directly where the checker can access the exact gathered version. Pass conversational material in full. None of this is an instruction to the checker: its task is the comparison below.

Save the complete current prose in a fresh scratch file and give the checker that exact file to read, with its own report path in the same scratch directory. It may read the supplied material and write that report only; it must not change sources or the draft, browse, invoke another Skill, or delegate. Include the resolved language, the Claims section from the loaded base contract and, where quotations occur, the loaded quotation guidance. Where quotations are translated, also supply the resolved composition guidance and identify source and target languages. Send this task without suggested findings or your explanation of the draft:

> Account for every factual and attributed claim in the complete draft, including headings and implications. Account separately for the person, number and natural-gender information conveyed by pronouns; identifying their referent does not establish those features. Distinguish natural-gender assertions from purely grammatical gender. Reconstruct each independently checkable proposition as a meaning-equivalent standalone statement, carrying over grammatical modifiers and qualifications that apply across clauses. For each, record the draft passage, that complete proposition and its supporting source passage. Write each proposition’s precise negation, keeping its subject and scope fixed. Identify the supplied statement that rules that negation out; otherwise give a concrete source-compatible counterexample. Test that exact proposition, including whose knowledge or assertion it describes. Distinguish factual assertions from advocacy and attributed interpretation. For each finding, show the support that is missing or changed and propose the smallest supported repair. Preserve supported claims, warranted certainty, voice and editorial choices. Judge source support. For translated quotations, separately check that the same meaning and distinctive voice are expressed in idiomatic target-language speech. Identify a concrete obstruction to that reading, not merely a preferred synonym; clarify an implicit referent only where the supplied context settles it. General editorial and mechanical review are outside this comparison. Distinguish source-support findings from translation findings. Write the complete claim accounting and findings to the report path, ending with completion status and any unresolved findings. Reply in at most 150 words with completion status and the report path.

Read the complete report and validate every finding yourself, after either comparison. First establish what the draft actually asserts in its full context, then whether the supplied material supports that proposition with its subject, scope and qualifications intact. A merely conceivable stronger reading does not establish a defect. Distinguish a report that has not established its allegation from genuine material ambiguity or unresolved support in the draft. Reject a finding only with exact draft and source evidence showing support or a concrete mismatch in the report’s reading. For a translation finding, use the resolved composition and quotation guidance to establish the target-language reading. Confidence, preferred wording or qualifications present only in the source settle neither kind of finding. Record each finding’s disposition and evidence beside the report.

Make only supported repairs, preserving the rest of the draft. If the first comparison leads to any change or rejected finding, give a fresh checker the complete current draft and original material for one final comparison under the same task. Supply neither the earlier findings nor your defence. There are at most two comparisons; validate the second report by the same standard, and make no unchecked prose changes after it.

Proceed only after a complete comparison of the current prose leaves no accepted defects or genuinely unresolved material claims. If comparison cannot finish, material cannot be supplied in full, or such findings remain after the second comparison, report the concrete obstacle or unresolved passages and stop without delivering the draft or writing it to the Output Target. Remove scratch, reports and dispositions on that exit too. A rejected finding is the writer’s evidenced decision, not the checker’s approval; a missing or partial report is never a completed comparison.

After a successful comparison, preserve the checked prose exactly; only the resolved Handoff Metadata and delivery wrapper remain to add. Read the report before removing its scratch directory. The report is internal working material, not an extra user deliverable.

# The base contract

Write with the clarity and factual precision of a well-edited newspaper or quality magazine. Genre, audience, and purpose override that register: a letter, a speech and an advertisement keep their own character. The selected genre governs craft and form; the resolved language governs idiom, syntax and typography. Examples here illustrate meanings, not English phrases to translate.

## Reader and progression

Give the intended reader what they need to understand, judge or do the thing the text is for. Keep a clear focus, introduce unfamiliar concepts before the reasoning needs them, and order material by that reader's needs rather than the writer's discovery process. Relevant technical detail belongs; unexplained jargon and unrelated background do not.

Make the relations between passages real. A transition may explain a connection, but cannot invent one. Keep paragraphs coherent and give supporting material a clear place beside what it supports. The body and its sections remain intelligible without treating a title, standfirst or subheading as their opening sentence.

Open on something specific to the subject. End with what the job calls for: an earned understanding, conclusion, recommendation or next step. Remove introductions and conclusions that add only an announcement or a generic flourish.

## Expression

Use concrete words, useful verbs and a natural, varied cadence. Keep terminology and reference clear; introduce an unfamiliar abbreviation before using it alone. Choose ordinary words where they suffice and established specialist terms where they give this reader precision.

Let tone and rhetorical devices serve the genre and the meaning. A useful analogy, question, image, fragment or humorous turn can clarify or carry a voice; decoration and manufactured drama cannot. An imagined comparison is recognisable as a comparison, never presented as an event or someone's experience. Criticism addresses the supported issue without inventing motives or patronising the reader.

Each passage earns its place. Repetition may establish an independent entry point, explain a hard idea or give a deliberate rhetorical return; merely saying the same thing again does none of these. Keep formatting useful: headings for orientation, lists for coordinate items, tables for comparisons, emphasis for what merits it. Hold voice, terminology and presentation consistent unless a visible purpose calls for a change.

## Claims

Every claim is supported by the text or its material, with exact attribution and proportionate strength. Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened. Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted. A fact, quotation, source, scene, personal experience or opinion attributed to somebody is never invented to complete a form. Name the actual source of an attributed claim rather than invoking unnamed studies or experts.

Circumstantial detail is a claim too: duration, manner, motive, absence and background all need support. So does an evaluative characterisation: calling a count high, low or modest needs a comparison, target, capacity or speaker assessment. Otherwise give the count with its exclusions, without that assessment.

A sequence or correlation establishes no cause. A causal verb such as *shortened* needs causal support; a causal hedge such as *suggests that it shortened* still adds that attribution. This boundary holds in the title, summary, headings and body alike. Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears.

A stated length constrains the use of material and is never a licence to add to it. When the material is insufficient, deliver the length the material supports and name what further material would close the gap. A supplied publication limit is binding; meeting it cannot justify invention or loss of a qualification that changes a claim.
# Craft for five web genres

For article, case-study, column and opinion, work as a skilled Swedish journalist at the professional level of SvD, DN, DI, Fokus, Ny Teknik, Filter or Forskning & Framsteg. For web-copy, work as an experienced Swedish copywriter and UX writer trusted by leading agencies and brands. These are standards of craft, not voices to imitate.

In every target language, keep that Swedish editorial or communicative tradition in the angle, disposition, storytelling, address and tone. Think and write wholly in the target language: its Language Resource governs vocabulary, idiom, syntax, punctuation and typography. A native professional should hear a colleague, not a translation. Language choice changes the language surface, not the chosen craft.

## Web reading

Give the reader a clear angle or task and useful ways into the text. Let facts and reasoning carry explanation; choose any narrative devices for what they contribute. Headings orient according to the genre, paragraphs hold connected thoughts, and varied rhythm supports both scanning and sustained reading.

Use these as scale guides: headings around 30–70 characters, an ingress around 60 words or fewer, and roughly 80 words as an upper guide for a paragraph; commonly 2–3 sentences per paragraph and 2–3 paragraphs per section. Genre, language, content and rhythm can justify different proportions. A successful departure needs neither permission nor explanation. Add or cut nothing just to reach a number; an actual brief or publication constraint still binds.

Where the genre calls for an ingress, make it a self-contained paragraph that tells readers what the piece offers. It may give the central result. The lead starts the body; it advances the account rather than replaying the ingress. Necessary overlap lets both work independently.

Elm Quay Housing testade en gemensam logg för felanmälningar i två byggnader. Underhållsteamet ville ge olika arbetsskift tillgång till samma information och utformade själva kategorierna. Elm Quay Housing förvaltar 640 lägenheter. Tidigare förvarades felanmälningar via telefon och mejl separat. I september 2025 beslutade bolagets eget underhållsteam att prova en gemensam logg under åtta veckor.

Underhållsteamet tog fram kategorierna och behöll möjligheten för de boende att felanmäla via telefon. Svale konfigurerade loggen och utbildade sex medarbetare vid två tillfällen.

För Lind gav arbetet en erfarenhet att ta med till nästa byggnad:

Mätningen gäller alltså tiden tills ett ärende tilldelades, inte tills reparationen var klar. Det saknas mätningar av kostnader, hur nöjda de boende var och tiden till slutförd reparation.

– Jag skulle välja att göra om försöket. Det hjälper oss att ha en samlad bild av felanmälningarna, men jag skulle avsätta en extra vecka för förberedelser.

Försöket har ännu inte utökats. Teamet ska först kontrollera hur kategorierna fungerar för större reparationer och därefter fatta beslut.

För dig som vill läsa vidare finns [Svale Systems checklista för införande](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).

*Den här kundberättelsen publiceras av leverantören Svale Systems.*
'''
(p/'draft.md').write_text(draft)
print(p)
print('Words:',len(draft.split()))
PY","max_output_tokens":1000}));

# Source and translated-quotation comparison

Read in full: source.md (complete brief and material), draft.md, and the supplied quotations.md. This report checks support and translated quotations only. Swedish is the target language. Statements about the fictional case are assessed against the supplied package, not external reality.

## Supporting source passages

- S1: “Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats.”
- S2: “In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings.”
- S3: “Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately. The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information.”
- S4: “It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.”
- S5: “The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents.”
- S6: “Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions. The trial lasted eight weeks.”
- S7: “Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.”
- S8: “Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.”
- S9: “There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements.”
- S10: “Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind, complete usable quotations”.
- Q1: “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”
- Q2: “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”
- Q3: “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”
- S11: “Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. It is not an inference from the figures.”
- S12: “The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs.”
- S13: “The supplier approved publication of this case as supplier-published material; it is not independent journalism. All interviews occurred by email”.
- S14: Brief: “The publisher is the supplier, Svale Systems”; “The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read”.

## Complete proposition accounting

Each row supplies the draft passage, its standalone proposition, its precise negation, and the source statement ruling out that negation. Repeated claims are recorded where they recur. Attributed wishes, testimony and evaluation remain attributed: support for a speaker's assertion is not treated as independent proof of its content.

Smallest supported repair: “Lind skulle avsätta mer tid för förberedelser”. An explicit alternative is “Lind skulle avsätta en extra vecka vid ett nytt försök”.

- Q2 preserves the greater time spent agreeing on categories versus first entries, the backward reference to that time, the conditional recommendation and its timing before the next building starts. “Nästa byggnad kommer i gång” preserves the source's metonymic reference in context and does not claim actual expansion. - The restrained, practical first-person voice survives all three translations. None adds a recommendation for every housing company or attributes a measured improvement to Lind. Her benefit assessment remains an assessment; it is not an inference from the figures.

All three translated quotations have been compared separately. Two unresolved source-support findings remain: F1 (planned versus actual duration) and F2 (conditional stance in heading). No files other than this report were written or changed.

# Source and translated-quotation comparison

Reviewed the complete supplied source and complete current draft, including title, standfirst, subheadings, link and publication disclosure. Applied the supplied Claims contract and quotation guidance. This report concerns source support and quotation translation only.

## Source key

The following identifiers refer to exact passages in the supplied source, not external material.

- B1: “Write a journalistic customer case for operations managers at small housing companies. The publisher is the supplier, Svale Systems. The customer, Elm Quay Housing, should remain the acting party.”
- B2: “The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial.”
- S1: “Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats.”
- S2: “In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings.”
- S3: “Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately.”
- S4: “The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information.”
- S5: “It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair.”
- S6: “No comparison with another supplier is available.”
- S7: “The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents.”
- S8: “Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions.”
- S9: “The trial lasted eight weeks.”
- S10: “Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered.”
- S11: “It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.”
- S12: “Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period.”
- S13: “The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.”
- S14: “There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements.”
- Q0: “Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind, complete usable quotations:”
- Q1: “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”
- Q2: “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”
- Q3: “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”
- S15: “Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. It is not an inference from the figures.”
- S16: “The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs.”
- S17: “The supplier approved publication of this case as supplier-published material; it is not independent journalism.”
- S18: “All interviews occurred by email, and no physical scene, emotion or remembered dialogue is provided. Translation of the quotations is permitted, preserving stance and qualification.”

## Complete proposition accounting

Each numbered entry gives the draft passage, a standalone meaning-equivalent proposition, its precise negation with subject and scope retained, and the supplied statement excluding that negation. Repeated appearances are listed together only where they express the same proposition. Reported intentions and opinions remain statements about the named person's or team's intentions and opinions; they are not converted into objective efficacy claims. The propositions drawn from translated quotations retain their attribution to Lind.

1. **Title: “Elm Quay fick en gemensam överblick över felanmälningarna”.** Proposition: Elm Quay obtained a shared view of the repair reports in the trial. Negation: Elm Quay did not obtain a shared view of the repair reports in the trial. Support: S2 establishes the shared log and Q3 explicitly describes the customer as having one view of the reports. Together these rule out the negation. The title does not assert that the software caused a performance improvement.

2. **Standfirst: “Elm Quay Housing testade en gemensam logg för felanmälningar i två byggnader.”** Proposition: Elm Quay Housing trialled a shared repair-report log in two buildings. Negation: Elm Quay Housing did not trial a shared repair-report log in two buildings. Support: S2 identifies the trial, customer, shared log and two-building scope; S9 and S10 establish that the intended trial took place. Supported.

3. **Standfirst: “Underhållsteamet ville ge olika arbetsskift tillgång till samma information”.** Proposition: Elm Quay's maintenance team wanted staff on different shifts to have access to the same information. Negation: Elm Quay's maintenance team did not want staff on different shifts to have access to the same information. Support: S4 states that intention. This does not claim independently measured information access or universal use. Supported.

4. **Standfirst: “utformade själva kategorierna”; subheading “Teamet utformade kategorierna”; body “Underhållsteamet tog fram kategorierna”.** Proposition: Elm Quay's maintenance team itself designed the categories used in the repair log. Negation: Elm Quay's maintenance team did not itself design the categories used in the repair log. Support: S7 and Q1. “Själva” preserves customer authorship without asserting that Svale had no implementation role. Supported.

5. **Standfirst: “Underhållsansvariga Maya Lind”.** Proposition: Maya Lind is the customer's maintenance supervisor. Negation: Maya Lind is not the customer's maintenance supervisor. Support: Q0. The Swedish role description is a supported ordinary rendering of this role, without adding a higher rank or a new responsibility. Supported.

6. **Standfirst: “Maya Lind skulle göra om försöket”; final quotation “Jag skulle välja att göra om försöket”.** Proposition: Lind says that she would choose to undertake the trial again. Negation: Lind does not say that she would choose to undertake the trial again. Support: Q3 states that exact qualified preference. Neither passage asserts a scheduled repeat trial. Supported.

7. **Standfirst: “men avsätta mer tid för förberedelser”; subheading “Lind skulle avsätta mer tid för förberedelser”.** Proposition: Lind's preference for another trial includes allowing more preparation time than before. Negation: Lind's preference for another trial does not include allowing more preparation time than before. Support: Q3 specifies an extra week; S15 describes this as her actual qualified assessment. The general paraphrase preserves the reservation, and the body supplies its exact size. Supported.

8. **Standfirst: “Något beslut om att utöka försöket har ännu inte fattats.”** Proposition: At the time described, the team has not yet decided whether to expand the trial. Negation: At the time described, the team has already decided whether to expand the trial. Support: S16 says that the team “will decide after checking” the larger-repair categories. It is this expressly future decision, not simply the lack of expansion, that excludes the negation. Supported.

9. **“Elm Quay Housing förvaltar 640 lägenheter.”** Proposition: Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. Negation: Elm Quay Housing does not manage 640 flats. Support: S1. Supported.

10. **“Tidigare förvarades felanmälningar via telefon och mejl separat.”** Proposition: Before the trial, telephone repair reports and emailed repair reports were stored separately. Negation: Before the trial, telephone repair reports and emailed repair reports were not stored separately. Support: S3 in the repair-log context established by S2. No unsupported claim of lost reports or customer incompetence is added. Supported.

11. **“I september 2025 beslutade bolagets eget underhållsteam att prova en gemensam logg.”** Proposition: In September 2025, Elm Quay Housing's own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log. Negation: In September 2025, Elm Quay Housing's own maintenance team did not decide to trial a shared repair log. Support: S2 supplies date, ownership, actor and decision. This sentence does not independently assert an exact trial start date. Supported.

12. **“Försöket pågick i åtta veckor.”** Proposition: The trial lasted eight weeks. Negation: The trial did not last eight weeks. Support: S9. Supported.

13. **Quotation: “Vi ville att kvällsskiftet skulle se vad morgonskiftet redan hade gjort.”** Proposition: Lind says that her team wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. Negation: Lind does not say that her team wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. Support: Q1, with the team referent settled by S4 and S7. The relative chronology conveyed by “redan” is in “already”. The quotation asserts an intention, not proof that every evening worker actually saw every morning action. Supported.

14. **Quotation: “Kategorierna var våra”.** Proposition: Lind says that the categories belonged to her team's work and were the team's own categories. Negation: Lind does not say that the categories were her team's own categories. Support: Q1 directly and S7 for the category-design context. This is attribution of category ownership/authorship, not an invented legal intellectual-property claim. Supported.

15. **Quotation: “Svale hjälpte oss att lägga in dem i loggen”.** Proposition: Lind says that Svale helped her team put its categories into the repair log. Negation: Lind does not say that Svale helped her team put its categories into the repair log. Support: Q1, with “them” and “dem” both referring to categories. Supported.

16. **“berättar Maya Lind i en mejlintervju”.** Proposition: Maya Lind supplied the quoted remarks in an email interview. Negation: Maya Lind did not supply the quoted remarks in an email interview. Support: Q0 identifies the interviewee and S18 states that all interviews occurred by email. No physical encounter, remembered dialogue or observable emotion is manufactured. Supported.

17. **“Teamet valde Svale Systems efter att ha testat om loggen kunde visa statusen för varje reparation.”** Proposition: Elm Quay's maintenance team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could display each repair's status. Negation: Elm Quay's maintenance team did not choose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could display each repair's status. Support: S5. The sentence preserves sequence and the question tested; it does not claim that a supplier comparison demonstrated superiority. Supported.

18. **“Underlaget innehåller ingen jämförelse med någon annan leverantör.”** Proposition: The supplied case material contains no comparison with another supplier. Negation: The supplied case material contains a comparison with another supplier. Support: S6, together with the complete supplied package. The draft limits this absence to the material and does not claim that the customer never compared suppliers. Supported.

19. **“behöll möjligheten för de boende att felanmäla via telefon”.** Proposition: Elm Quay's maintenance team kept telephone repair reporting available to residents during the trial. Negation: Elm Quay's maintenance team did not keep telephone repair reporting available to residents during the trial. Support: S7. Supported.

20. **“Svale konfigurerade loggen”.** Proposition: Svale configured the repair log for the trial. Negation: Svale did not configure the repair log for the trial. Support: S8. Supported.

21. **“utbildade sex medarbetare vid två tillfällen”.** Proposition: Svale trained six staff over two training sessions. Negation: Svale did not train six staff over two training sessions. Support: S8 supplies both numbers and the activity. The draft does not say there were twelve trainees or specify session duration. Supported.

22. **“För Lind gav arbetet en erfarenhet att ta med till nästa byggnad”.** Proposition: Lind's account of the category work includes an experience that informs her stated preparation choice for the next building. Negation: Lind's account of the category work includes no experience informing her stated preparation choice for the next building. Support: Q2 expressly connects the time spent agreeing categories to setting aside “that time” before the next building starts. This introductory characterisation attributes the lesson to Lind; it neither invents an emotion nor asserts that expansion is approved. Supported.

23. **Quotation: “Vi lade mer tid på att komma överens om kategorierna än på att registrera de första felanmälningarna.”** Proposition: Lind says that her team spent more time agreeing the categories than entering the first repair reports. Negation: Lind does not say that her team spent more time agreeing the categories than entering the first repair reports. Support: Q2. The comparison retains its two activities and its restriction to the first reports, without creating a measured duration. Supported.

24. **Quotation: “Jag skulle avsätta den tiden innan nästa byggnad kommer i gång.”** Proposition: Lind says that she would reserve the time needed to agree the categories before work with the trial/log begins in the next building. Negation: Lind does not say that she would reserve the time needed to agree the categories before work with the trial/log begins in the next building. Support: Q2 (“that time”, “before the next building starts”), interpreted within S2 and S16. This preserves the source's contextual building-as-activity shorthand and hypothetical “would”. It does not state that another building has already started or has been approved. Supported.

25. **Subheading: “Kortare tid till tilldelning under försöket”.** Proposition: In the trial, the reported report-to-assignment time was shorter than in the comparison period, as measured by the median identified in the section. Negation: In the trial, the reported report-to-assignment time was not shorter than in the comparison period, as measured by that median. Support: S12's two-versus-three working days establishes the decrease. The heading uses assignment, not completion, and contains no causal verb or supplier agency. Its section immediately states the median, the comparison and the limitation. Supported.

26. **“Elm Quays interna försöksanteckning, daterad den 4 december 2025”.** Proposition: Elm Quay has an internal trial note dated 4 December 2025. Negation: Elm Quay does not have an internal trial note dated 4 December 2025. Support: S10. “Elm Quay” is an unambiguous shortened customer name. Supported.

27. **“Enligt … registrerades 31 felanmälningar.”** Proposition: Elm Quay's internal trial note dated 4 December 2025 says 31 repair reports were entered for the trial, within the exclusions stated immediately afterward. Negation: Elm Quay's internal trial note dated 4 December 2025 does not say 31 repair reports were entered for the trial within those exclusions. Support: S10 and S11. The draft does not present the note as independent validation or call the count high or low. Supported.

28. **“Akuta ärenden … ingår inte i underlaget.”** Proposition: The trial note's reporting/measurement material excludes emergencies. Negation: The trial note's reporting/measurement material includes emergencies. Support: S11. “Underlaget” here is locally the note's trial material; it does not deny the existence of emergency work. Supported.

29. **“arbeten som beställts före försöket ingår inte i underlaget”.** Proposition: The trial note's reporting/measurement material excludes work ordered before the trial. Negation: The trial note's reporting/measurement material includes work ordered before the trial. Support: S11. The modifier “före försöket” attaches to ordering, exactly as in the source; it has not become a restriction on when work finished. Supported.

30. **“Mediantiden från felanmälan till tilldelning var två arbetsdagar under försöket”.** Proposition: Within the trial note's stated reporting scope, the median elapsed time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial. Negation: Within that scope, the median elapsed time from report to assignment was not two working days during the trial. Support: S10–S12. The full metric, unit, period and exclusions are preserved. Supported.

31. **“jämfört med tre under den föregående åttaveckorsperioden”.** Proposition: Within the reported comparison, the median elapsed time from report to assignment was three working days in the eight-week period preceding the trial. Negation: Within that comparison, the median elapsed time from report to assignment was not three working days in the eight-week period preceding the trial. Support: S12. “Median”, “from report to assignment” and “working days” carry across the coordination; none is dropped in this reconstructed proposition. Supported.

32. **“Arbetsbelastningen skilde sig mellan perioderna.”** Proposition: The trial period and preceding eight-week comparison period had different workloads. Negation: Those two periods did not have different workloads. Support: S13. No direction or magnitude of the workload difference is added. Supported.

33. **“Anteckningen tillskriver uttryckligen inte programvaran skillnaden.”** Proposition: The internal note expressly does not attribute the observed median assignment-time difference to the software. Negation: It is not the case that the internal note expressly does not attribute that difference to the software. Support: S13 uses the same explicit non-attribution. The proposition concerns what the note attributes; it does not claim that the software is known to have had no effect. Supported.

34. **“Mätningen gäller alltså tiden tills ett ärende tilldelades, inte tills reparationen var klar.”** Proposition: The time measurement described measures report-to-assignment time, not repair-completion time. Negation: The time measurement described is not a report-to-assignment measurement distinct from repair-completion time. Support: S12 names the assignment endpoint and S14 states that there are no completion-time measurements. This clarification does not imply an unmeasured completion result. Supported.

35. **“Det saknas mätningar av kostnader”.** Proposition: The supplied trial evidence contains no cost measurements. Negation: The supplied trial evidence contains cost measurements. Support: S14. In the immediate discussion of the note and its measurements, this is an evidence-availability claim, not a claim that costs did not change. Supported.

36. **“[Det saknas mätningar av] hur nöjda de boende var”.** Proposition: The supplied trial evidence contains no resident-satisfaction measurements. Negation: The supplied trial evidence contains resident-satisfaction measurements. Support: S14. No resident sentiment is invented. Supported.

37. **“[Det saknas mätningar av] tiden till slutförd reparation”.** Proposition: The supplied trial evidence contains no repair-completion-time measurements. Negation: The supplied trial evidence contains repair-completion-time measurements. Support: S14. Supported.

38. **“Linds egen bedömning av försöket rymmer ett förbehåll”.** Proposition: The following assessment is Lind's own qualified assessment of the trial. Negation: The following assessment is not Lind's own qualified assessment of the trial. Support: S15 explicitly supplies both ownership and qualification; Q3 supplies the reservation. The draft does not infer Lind's assessment from the numerical results. Supported.

39. **Quotation: “Det hjälper oss att ha en samlad bild av felanmälningarna”.** Proposition: Lind says that having a single view of the repair reports helps her team. Negation: Lind does not say that having a single view of the repair reports helps her team. Support: Q3. This is a directly attributed practical assessment, with warranted affirmative certainty, not a measured causal claim about assignment times, costs or resident satisfaction. Supported.

40. **Quotation: “men jag skulle avsätta en extra vecka för förberedelser”.** Proposition: Lind says that, although she would choose to do the trial again and finds the shared view helpful, she would allow one extra week for preparation. Negation: Lind does not say that, despite those positive assessments, she would allow one extra week for preparation. Support: Q3 preserves the conjunction, first-person preference and exact additional period. Supported.

41. **“Försöket har ännu inte utökats.”** Proposition: At the time described, the trial has not expanded. Negation: At the time described, the trial has expanded. Support: S16. Supported.

42. **“Teamet ska först kontrollera hur kategorierna fungerar för större reparationer och därefter fatta beslut.”** Proposition: Elm Quay's team will check how the categories work for larger repairs before deciding whether to expand the trial. Negation: Elm Quay's team will not check how the categories work for larger repairs before deciding whether to expand the trial. Support: S16 supplies future checking, larger-repair scope and decision order. In context “fatta beslut” refers to expansion, not a decision to purchase already made. The text leaves the eventual decision open. Supported.

43. **“För dig som vill läsa vidare finns [Svale Systems checklista för införande](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).”** Proposition: The supplied URL is an implementation checklist associated with Svale Systems, offered as an optional document for further reading. Negation: The supplied URL is not an implementation checklist associated with Svale Systems offered as an optional document for further reading. Support: B2 supplies the document type, exact URL and optional reading purpose, in the supplier-published brief B1. The conditional invitation makes no assertion that any particular reader wants to read it. It does not promise a consultation, trial or checklist results. Supported.

44. **Disclosure: “Den här kundberättelsen publiceras av leverantören Svale Systems.”** Proposition: This customer case is published as supplier material by Svale Systems, which is the supplier. Negation: This customer case is not published as supplier material by Svale Systems, the supplier. Support: B1 and S17. The journalistic form is not represented as editorial independence. Supported.

## Pronoun and person/number/gender accounting

This accounting separates reference from the grammatical or natural-person information expressed. None of these expressions requires an unsupported inference from Maya's name.

- **“själva”** in the standfirst: reflexive/intensive reference is the maintenance-team members acting as a group. It expresses their own agency and semantic plurality, without natural gender. S2 establishes a team, S7 its authorship and S8 explicitly establishes multiple trained staff. “Själva” is not an assertion that the supplier gave no help. Negation of the relevant assertion: the categories were not the team's own work. S7 and Q1 exclude it.
- **“Vi”** in quotations 1 and 2: first-person plural, including speaker Lind and a group; no natural-gender feature. The source has “We” in precisely both places. The team referent is settled by the interview and category context; person and number are independently supported by the actual first-person plural source wording. Negation: Lind's quoted “we” does not denote herself with a plural group in these statements. Q1 and Q2 exclude it.
- **“våra”** in quotation 1: first-person plural possessor; the categories are plural possessed items; no natural-gender assertion. Q1 “ours” independently supports the possessor person and number, and “categories” supports plurality of the possessed items. Negation: Lind does not present the plural categories as belonging to her first-person plural group. Q1 excludes it.
- **“oss”** in quotations 1 and 3: first-person plural object, speaker included, no natural gender. The source explicitly uses “us” in both passages. Negation: Lind does not describe her first-person plural group as recipient of Svale's assistance / beneficiary of the shared view, respectively. Q1 / Q3 exclude the corresponding negation.
- **“dem”** in quotation 1: third-person plural object referring to the categories, no natural gender. Q1's “them”, linked to “categories”, supplies reference and plurality separately. Negation: the quoted assistance concerns putting something other than the plural categories into the log. Q1 excludes it.
- **“Jag/jag”** in quotations 2 and 3: first-person singular Lind, no natural gender. Q2 and Q3 explicitly use “I”. Negation: the stated preparation choice / willingness to repeat / extra-week choice is not presented by Lind as her own individual choice. The respective source “I would” excludes each version of that negation.
- **“den tiden”** in quotation 2: singular demonstrative with Swedish common grammatical gender, referring to time for agreeing categories. It does not encode anybody's natural gender. Q2 “that time” supports the reference; time is a mass concept rather than a headcount. Negation: the time Lind would reserve is not the previously mentioned category-agreement time. Q2's linked sentences exclude it.
- **“sig”** in “Arbetsbelastningen skilde sig”: third-person reflexive in the Swedish expression for differed, carrying no independent number or natural-gender claim about a person. Its subject is workload. S13 supplies the asserted difference. Negation and support are recorded in entry 32.
- **“Det”** in “Det saknas mätningar”: impersonal syntactic subject, no person, number or natural-gender assertion concerning an entity. The evidence-absence claims are individually recorded in entries 35–37.
- **“Det”** in “Det hjälper oss att ha …”: anticipatory subject for the infinitive describing having one view. It adds no person or natural-gender information and makes no separate claim of an identified neuter object helping the team. Entry 39 captures the proposition supported by Q3.
- **“dig”** in the optional link sentence: singular second-person reader address, gender-neutral. It is a conditional invitation, not a factual assertion that there is exactly one reader or that the actual reader has a specified natural gender. B2 authorizes the optional reading invitation.
- **“Den här”** in the disclosure: singular demonstrative, common grammatical gender determined by “kundberättelsen”. The referent is the present text. B1 and S17 establish its supplier-publication status; no human gender is asserted.
- **“Något”** in the no-decision sentence: neuter indefinite determiner matching the grammatical gender of “beslut”. It contributes the negative existential claim about a decision in entry 8; no natural gender is involved.
- **“de boende”**: plural resident description, not a gendered personal pronoun. The source's “residents” expressly supports plurality. Neither phrase makes a natural-gender claim. Telephone availability and absent satisfaction measurements are supported by S7 and S14.
- **“Underhållsansvariga Maya Lind”**: this role adjective's -a form is not an independent assertion of female natural gender; Swedish uses this form without restricting the named person to a natural gender. The role is supported by Q0. The draft otherwise avoids “hon”, “han”, “hennes” and “hans”. In any event, the source itself calls the final quotation “Her final quotation”, so female reference would not depend solely on the name.
- **“Linds”, “Elm Quays”, “bolagets”, “Svale Systems”** possessive/naming constructions: these are named or nominal references, not gendered possessive pronouns. They add no natural-gender information. The customer/team relationship is explicit in S2; the note ownership is explicit in S10; Lind's assessment ownership is explicit in S15.
